inputs.voiceTranscript: Alright everyone, let us settle in. Today we are tackling one of the most fundamental challenges in computer science: distributed consensus in asynchronous networks. Why is consensus so hard? Because networks are unreliable: messages can be dropped, delayed arbitrarily, or reordered, and server nodes can crash without notice! Remember the CAP Theorem: when a network partition happens, a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability. For systems that choose consistency, like replicated state machines, we need a consensus protocol. Paxos was the original solution, but as Ongaro and Ousterhout pointed out, Paxos is notoriously difficult to understand and implement. That is why they created Raft. Raft decomposes distributed consensus into three distinct, manageable subproblems: leader election, log replication, and safety. Today we focus specifically on leader election. In Raft, at any given moment, each server node is in one of three states: follower, candidate, or leader. Normally, there is exactly one leader, and all other nodes are followers. The leader sends periodic heartbeats—which are empty AppendEntries Remote Procedure Calls—to all followers. Followers remain passive as long as they receive regular heartbeats. But what happens if the leader crashes? Let me ask Rahul in the second row: what does a follower do when heartbeats stop arriving? Exactly: the follower times out and transitions to the candidate state! The candidate increments its current term counter, votes for itself, and broadcasts RequestVote RPCs to every other node in the cluster. To become the leader, the candidate must win votes from a strict majority of nodes—meaning more than N divided by two, or at least floor of N over two plus one. But now think about this critical failure mode: what if two or three followers time out at the exact same instant? Suppose we have a five-node cluster, and two followers time out simultaneously. Node A gets two votes, Node B gets two votes, and Node C gets one vote. Neither candidate achieves a majority quorum of three votes! This is called a split vote. If all nodes had identical fixed timeout intervals, they would time out again at the exact same time, split the vote again, and stay stuck in an infinite election loop! How does Raft solve split-vote deadlocks? Listen carefully, this is a classic exam question: Raft uses randomized election timeouts! Instead of a fixed timer, each node randomly chooses an election timeout from a predefined interval, typically 150 to 300 milliseconds. Because the timeouts are randomized, one node will almost certainly time out before the others. It immediately transitions to candidate, increments the term, and collects votes from the remaining followers before their timers expire! And finally, what about the safety rule? What if a candidate was disconnected for a while, missed several committed log entries, and then wakes up and asks for votes? Raft enforces the Leader Completeness property: a voter must deny its vote if the candidate log is less up-to-date than the voter own log. If the candidate last log term is lower, or if terms are equal but its log length is shorter, the vote is rejected. This guarantees that any node that wins an election already contains every committed entry from all previous terms.
